लाजवंती

"हथ लाइयाँ कुम्हलाँनी लाजवंती दे बूटे !" (यह छुई-मुई के पौधे हैं री, हाथ भी लगाओ तो कुम्हला जाते हैं।) —एक पंजाबी गीत

बँटवारा हुआ और बेशुमार ज़ख़्मी लोगों ने उठकर अपने बदन पर से खून पोंछ डाला और फिर सब मिलकर उनकी तरफ मुतवज्जह' हो गए जिनके बदन सही व सालिम थे, लेकिन दिल ज़ख़्मी।

गली-गली, मुहल्ले-मुहल्ले में 'फिर बसाओ' कमेटियाँ बन गई थीं और शुरू-शुरू में बड़ी तनदही' के साथ 'कारोबार में बसाओ', 'ज़मीन पर बसाओ' और 'घरों में बसाओ' प्रोग्राम शुरू कर दिया गया था। लेकिन एक प्रोग्राम ऐसा था जिसकी तरफ किसी ने तवज्जह न दी थी। वह प्रोग्राम मुग़विया' औरतों के सिलसिले में था, जिसका स्लोगन था 'दिल में बसाओ'। और इस प्रोग्राम की नारायण बावा के मंदिर और उसके आसपास बसनेवाले क़दामतपसंद' तबके की तरफ से बड़ी मुखालफत होती थी इस प्रोग्राम को हरकत में लाने के लिए मंदिर के पास मुहल्ले 'मुल्ला शकूर' में एक कमेटी कायम हो गई और ग्यारह वोटों की अकसरियत' से सुंदरलाल बाबू को उसका सेक्रेटरी चुन लिया गया। वकील साहब सदर, चौकी कलाँ का बूढ़ा मुहर्रिर और मुहल्ले के दूसरे मातबर लोगों का खयाल था कि सुंदरलाल से ज़्यादा जॉफ़िशानी' के साथ उस काम को कोई और न कर सकेगा। शायद इसलिए कि सुंदरलाल की अपनी बीवी अगवा हो चुकी थी और उसका नाम था भी लाजो, लाजवंती।

चुनांचे प्रभातफेरी निकालते हुए जब सुंदरलाल बाबू, उसका साथी रसालू और नेकीराम वगैरह मिलकर गाते : "हथ लाइयाँ कुम्हलाँनी लाजवंती दे बूटे” तो सुंदरलाल की आवाज़ एकदम बंद हो जाती और वह खामोशी के साथ चलते-चलते लाजवंती की बाबत सोचता : 'जाने वह कहाँ होगी, किस हाल में होगी, हमारी बाबत क्या सोच रही होगी, वह कभी आएगी भी या नहीं ?' और पथरीले फर्श पर चलते-चलते उसके कदम लड़खड़ाने लगते। और अब तो यहाँ तक नौबत आ गई थी कि उसने लाजवंती के बारे में सोचना ही छोड़ दिया था। उसका ग़म अब दुनिया का ग़म हो चुका था। उसने अपने दुख से बचने

1. ध्यानाकर्षित; 2. एकाग्रता; 3. ध्यान; 4. अपहृत; 5. रूढ़िवादी; 6. बहुमत; 7. समर्पण-भावना।

बेदी समग्र - 2/227

के लिए लोकसेवा में अपने-आपको ग़र्क कर दिया। इसके बावजूद दूसरे साथियों की आवाज़ में आवाज़ मिलाते हुए उसे यह खयाल ज़रूर आता, इनसानी दिल कितना नाजुक होता है। ज़रा सी बात पर उसे ठेस लग सकती है। वह लाजवंती के पौधे की तरह है, जिसकी तरफ हाथ भी बढ़ाओ तो कुम्हला जाता है। लेकिन उसने अपनी लाजवंती के साथ बदसुलूकी करने में कोई भी कसर न उठा रखी थी। वह उसे जगह-बेजगह उठने-बैठने, खाने की तरफ बेतवज्जही' बरतने और ऐसी ही मामूली-मामूली बातों पर पीट दिया करता था। और लाजो एक पतली शहतूत की डाल की तरह नाजुक सी देहाती लड़की थी। ज़्यादा धूप देखने की वजह से उसका रंग सँवला चुका था। तबीयत में एक अजीब तरह की बेकारी थी। उसका इज़्तराब शबनम के उस कतरे की तरह था जो पारा किरास के बड़े से पत्ते पर कभी इधर कभी उधर लुढ़कता रहता है। उसका दुबलापन उसकी सेहत के खराब होने की दलील न थी। एक सेहतमंदी की निशानी थी, जिसे देखकर भारी-भरकम सुंदरलाल पहले तो घबराया, लेकिन जब उसने देखा कि लाजो हर किस्म का बोझ, हर किस्म का सदमा, हत्ता कि' मार-पीट तक सह गुज़रती है तो वह अपनी बदसुलूकी को ब-तदरीज⁴ बढ़ाता गया और उसने उन हदों का खयाल भी न किया, जहाँ पहुँच जाने के बाद किसी भी इनसान का सब्र टूट सकता है। इन हदों को धुँधला देने में लाजवंती खुद भी तो ममद⁵ साबित हुई थी। चूँकि वह देर तक उदास न बैठ सकती थी इसलिए बड़ी से बड़ी लड़ाई के बाद भी सुंदरलाल के सिर्फ एक बार मुस्कुरा देने पर वह अपनी हँसी न रोक सकती और लपककर उसके पास चली आती और गले में बाँहें डालते हुए कह उठती : "फिर मारा तो मैं तुमसे नहीं बोलूँगी।" साफ पता चलता था, वह एकदम सारी मारपीट भूल चुकी है। गाँव की दूसरी लड़कियों की तरह वह भी जानती थी कि मर्द ऐसा ही सुलूक किया करते हैं, बल्कि औरतों में कोई भी सरकशी करती तो लड़कियाँ खुद ही नाक पर उँगली रखके कहतीं : 'ले वह भी कोई मर्द है भला, औरत जिसके काबू में नहीं आती' और यह मारपीट उनके गीतों में चली गई थी। खुद लाजो गाया करती थी : 'मैं शहर के लड़के से शादी न करूँगी। वह बूट पहनता है और मेरी कमर बड़ी पतली है।' लेकिन पहली ही फुर्सत में लाजो ने शहर ही के एक लड़के से लौ लगा ली और उसका नाम था सुंदरलाल, जो एक बरात के साथ लाजवंती के गाँव चला आया था और जिसने दूल्हा के कान में सिर्फ इतना सा कहा था : 'तेरी साली तो बड़ी नमकीन है यार, बीवी भी चटपटी होगी।' लाजवंती ने सुंदरलाल की इस बात को सुन लिया था, मगर वह यह भूल ही गई की सुंदरलाल कितने बड़े-बड़े और भद्दे बूट पहने हुए है और उसकी अपनी कमर कितनी पतली है !

और प्रभातफेरी के समय ऐसी ही बातें सुंदरलाल को याद आतीं और वह यही सोचता : एक बार, सिर्फ एक बार लाजो मिल जाए तो मैं सचमुच ही दिल में बसा लूँ और लोगों को बता दूँ कि इन बिचारी औरतों के अगवा हो जाने में उनका कोई कुसूर नहीं। फ़सादियों की हवसनाकियों⁷ का शिकार हो जाने में उनकी कोई ग़लती नहीं। वह 1. उपेक्षा; 2. बेचैनी; 3. यहाँ तक कि; 4. क्रमशः; 5. सहायक; 6. उदंडता; 7. लोलुपताओं ।

228 / बेदी समग्र - 2

समाज जो इन मासूम और बेकुसूर औरतों को कुबूल नहीं करता, उन्हें अपना नहीं लेता. एक गला-सड़ा समाज है और उसे ख़त्म कर देना चाहिए वह उन औरतों को घरों में आबाद करने की तलकीन' किया करता और उन्हें ऐसा मर्तबा देने की प्रेरणा करता जो घर में किसी भी औरत, किसी भी माँ, बेटी, बहन या बीवी को दिया जाता है। फिर वह कहता : 'उन्हें इशारे और किनाए से² भी ऐसी बातों की याद नहीं दिलानी चाहिए जो उनके साथ हुईं; क्योंकि उनके दिल ज़ख़्मी हैं। वह नाजुक हैं, छुई मुई की तरह हाथ भी लगाओ तो कुम्हला जाएँगे ".'

गोया 'दिल में बसाओ' प्रोग्राम को अमली जामा पहनाने के लिए मुहल्ला मुल्ला शकूर की इस कमेटी ने कई प्रभातफेरियाँ निकालीं। सुब्ह चार-पाँच बजे का वक्त उनके लिए मौजूँतरीन³ वक़्त होता था। न लोगों का शोर, न ट्रैफिक की उलझन । रात-भर चौकीदारी करनेवाले कुत्ते तक बुझे हुए तनूरों में सर देकर पड़े होते थे। अपने-अपने बिस्तरों में दुबके हुए लोग प्रभातफेरीवालों की आवाज़ सुनकर सिर्फ इतना कहते : "ओ ! वही मंडली है !” और फिर कभी सब्र और कभी तुनकमिज़ाजी से वह बाबू सुंदरलाल का प्रोपेगेंडा सुना करते । वे औरतें जो बड़ी महफूज़⁴ उस पार पहुँच गई थीं, गोभी के फूलों की तरह फैली पड़ी रहतीं और उनके खाविंद उनके पहलू में डंठलों की तरह अकड़े पड़े-पड़े प्रभातफेरी⁵ के शोर पर एहतजार्ज⁶ करते हुए मुँह में कुछ मिनमिनाते चले जाते। या कहीं कोई बच्चा थोड़ी देर के लिए आँखें खोलता और 'दिल में बसाओ' के फ़रियादी और अंदोहगीं प्रोपेगेंडे को सिर्फ एक गाना समझ के फिर सो जाता ।

लेकिन सुब्ह के समय कान में पड़ा हुआ शब्द बेकार नहीं जाता। वह सारा दिन एक तकरार के साथ दिमाग़ में चक्कर लगाता रहता है और बाज़ वक़्त⁷ तो इनसान उसके मानी को भी नहीं समझता, पर गुनगुनाता चला जाता है। इसी आवाज़ के घर कर जाने की बदौतल ही, उन्हीं दिनों जबकि मिस मृदुला साराभाई हिंद और पाकिस्तान के दरमियान अगवाशुदा औरतें तबादले में लाईं तो मुहल्ला मुल्ला शकूर के कुछ आदमी उन्हें फिर से बसाने के लिए तैयार हो गए। उनके वारिस शहर से बाहर चौकी कलाँ पर उनसे मिलने के लिए गए। मुग़विया औरतें और उनके लवाहकीन⁸ कुछ देर एक-दूसरे को देखते रहे और फिर सिर झुकाए अपने-अपने बरबाद घरों को फिर से आबाद करने के काम पर चल दिए। रिसालू और नेकीराम और सुंदरलाल बाबू कभी 'महेंद्र सिंह जिंदाबाद' और कभी 'सोहनलाल जिंदाबाद' के नारे लगाते और वह नारे लगाते रहे, हत्ता कि उनके गले सूख गए

लेकिन मुग़विया औरतों में कुछ ऐसी भी थीं जिनके शौहरों, जिनके माँ, बाप, बहन और भाइयों ने उन्हें पहचानने से इनकार कर दिया था। आखिर वह मर क्यों न गईं ? अपनी इफ़्फ़त⁹ और इस्मत को बचाने के लिए उन्होंने ज़हर क्यों न खा लिया ? कुएँ में छलाँग क्यों न लगा दी ? वह बुज़दिल थीं जो इस तरह ज़िंदगी से चिमटी हुई थीं। सैकड़ों-हज़ारों औरतों ने इस्मत लुट जाने से पहले अपनी जान दे दी। लेकिन उन्हें क्या 1. उपदेश; 2. परोक्ष रूप से; 3. सबसे उपयुक्त; 4. सुरक्षित; 5. विरोध; 6. दुखद; 7. कभी-कभी; 8. रिश्तेदार; 9. पवित्रता ।

देखो देखो जितनी औरतें तुमने दी हैं उनमें से एक भी बराबरी करती है इसकी ?' और वहाँ लाजो भाभी सबकी नज़रों के सामने अपने तंदोले छुपा रही थी। "फिर झगड़ा बढ़ गया। दोनों ने अपना-अपना 'माल' वापस ले लेने की ठान ली। मैंने शोर मचाया : 'लाजो लाजो भाभी' मगर हमारी कौम के सिपाहियों ने हमें ही मार-मार के भगा दिया।" और लालचंद अपनी कोहनी दिखाने लगा, जहाँ उसे लाठी पड़ी थी। रसालू और नेकीराम चुपचाप बैठे रहे और सुंदरलाल कहीं दूर देखने लगा। शायद सोचने लगा, लाजो आई भी पर न आई और सुंदरलाल की शक्ल ही से जान पड़ता था जैसे वह बीकानेर का सेहरा' फाँदकर आया है और अब कहीं दरख़्त की छाँव में, ज़बान निकाले हाँफ रहा है। मुँह से इतना भी नहीं निकलता : 'पानी दे दो।' उसे यूँ महसूस हुआ, बँटवारे से पहले और बँटवारे के बाद का तशदुद अभी तक कारफ़रमा है। सिर्फ उसकी शक्ल बदल गई है। अब लोगों में पहला सा दरेग भी नहीं रहा। किसी से पूछो, साँभरवाला में लहनासिंह रहा करता था और उसकी भाभी बंतो वह तो झट से कहता, 'मर गए' और उसके बाद मौत और उसके मफहूम से बिलकुल बेखबर, बिलकुल आरी' आगे बढ़ता चला जाता। इससे भी एक कदम आगे बढ़कर बड़े ठंडे दिल से ताजिर इनसानी माल, इनसानी गोश्त और पोस्त की तिजारत और उसका तबादला करने लगे। मवेशी खरीदनेवाले किसी भैंस या गाय का जबड़ा खोलकर दाँतों से उसकी उम्र का अंदाज़ा करते थे। अब वह जवान औरत के रूप, उसके निखार, उसके अज़ीज़तरीन राज़ों, उसके तंदोलों की सरे-आम नुमाइश करने लगे। तशदुद अब ताजिरों की नस-नस में बस चुका है, पहले मंडी में माल बिकता था और भाव-ताव करनेवाले हाथ मिलाकर उस पर एक रूमाल डाल लेते और यूँ 'गुप्ती' कर लेते गोया रूमाल के नीचे उँगलियों के इशारों से सौदा हो जाता था। अब 'गुप्ती' का रूमाल भी हट चुका था और सामने सौदे हो रहे थे और लोग तिजारत के आदाब भी भूल गए थे। यह सारा लेन-देन, यह कारोबार पुराने ज़माने की दास्तान मालूम हो रहा था, जिसमें औरतों की आज़ादाना खरीदो-फरोख्त का किस्सा बयान किया जाता है। अज़-बयक अनगिनत उरियाँ औरतों के सामने खड़ा उनके जिस्मों को टोह-टोह के देख रहा है और जब वह किसी औरत के जिस्म को उँगली लगाता है तो

उस पर एक गुलाबी सा गढ़ा पड़ जाता है और उसके इर्द-गिर्द एक ज़र्द सा हलका' और फिर ज़र्दियाँ और सुर्खियाँ एक-दूसरे की जगह लेने के लिए दौड़ती हैं अज़-बयक आगे गुज़र जाता है और नाकाबिले-कुबूल औरत एक एतराफ़े-शिकस्त', एक इनफ़आलियत के आलम में एक हाथ से इज़ारबंद थामे और दूसरे से अपने चेहरे को अवाम की नज़रों से छिपाए सिसकियाँ लेती है।

सुंदरलाल अमृतसर (सरहद) जाने की तैयारी कर ही रहा था कि उसे लाजो के आने की खबर मिली। एकदम से ऐसी खबर मिल जाने से सुंदरलाल घबरा गया। उसका एक कदम फौरन दरवाज़े की तरफ बढ़ा लेकिन वह पीछे लौट आया। उसका जी चाहता था कि वह रूठ जाए और कमेटी के तमाम प्लेकार्डों और झंडियों को बिछाकर बैठ जाए और फिर रोए। लेकिन वहाँ जज़्बात का यूँ मुज़ाहिरा मुमकिन न था। उसने मर्दाना-वार इस अंदरूनी कशमकश का मुकाबला किया और अपने कदमों को नापते हुए चौकी कलाँ की तरफ चल दिया, क्योंकि वही जगह थी, जहाँ मग़विया औरतों की डिलीवरी दी जाती थी। अब लाजो सामने खड़ी थी और एक ख़ौफ़ के जज़्बे से काँप रही थी। वही सुंदरलाल को जानती थी, उसके सिवाय कोई न जानता था। वह पहले ही उसके साथ ऐसा सुलूक करता था और अब जबकि वह एक गैर मर्द के साथ ज़िंदगी के दिन बिताकर आई थी, न जाने क्या करेगा ? सुंदरलाल ने लाजो की तरफ देखा। वह खालिस इस्लामी तर्ज़ का लाल दुप‌ट्टा ओढ़े थी और बाएँ बुक्कल मारे हुए थी आदतन, महज़ आदतन दूसरी औरतों में घुलमिल जाने और बिल-आखिर अपने सैयाद के दाम से भाग जाने की आसानी थी। और वह सुंदरलाल के बारे में इतना ज़्यादा सोच रही थी कि उसे कपड़े बदलने या दुपट्टा ठीक से ओढ़ने का भी ख़याल न रहा। वह हिंदू और मुसलमान तहज़ीब के बुनियादी फ़र्क दाएँ बुक्कल और बाएँ बुक्कल में इम्तियाज़ करने से कासिर" रही थी। अब वह सुंदरलाल के सामने खड़ी थी और काँप रही थी, एक उम्मीद और एक डर के जज़्बे के साथ- सुंदरलाल को धक्का-सा लगा। उसने देखा, लाजवंती का रंग कुछ निखर गया था और वह पहले की बनिस्बत कुछ तनदुरुस्त सी नज़र आती थी। नहीं, वह मोटी हो गई थी सुंदरलाल ने जो कुछ लाजो के बारे में सोच रखा था वह सब ग़लत था। वह समझता था, ग़म में घुल जाने के बाद लाजवंती बिलकुल मरियल हो चुकी होगी और आवाज़ उसके मुँह से निकाले न निकलती होगी। इस खयाल से कि वह पाकिस्तान में बड़ी खुश रही है, उसे बड़ा सदमा हुआ। लेकिन वह चुप रहा, क्योंकि उसने चुप रहने की कसम खा रखी थी। अगरचे वह न जान पाया कि इतनी खुश थी तो फिर चली क्यों आई ? उसने सोचा : 'शायद हिंद सरकार के दबाव की वजह से अपनी मर्जी के खिलाफ यहाँ आना पड़ा' लेकिन एक चीज़ वह न समझ सका कि लाजवंती का सँवलाया हुआ चेहरा ज़र्दी लिए हुए था और ग़म, महज़ ग़म से उसके बदन के गोश्त ने हड्डियों को छोड़ दिया था। बह ग़म की कसरत' से मोटी हो गई थी और सेहतमंद नज़र आती थी। लेकिन यह ऐसी सेहतमंदी थी जिसमें दो कदम चलने पर आदमी का साँस फूल जाता है मुग़विया के चेहरे पर पहली निगाह डालने पर तास्सुर' कुछ अजीब सा हुआ। लेकिन उसने सब खयालात का एक इसबाती' मर्दानगी से मुकाबला किया। और भी बहुत से लोग मौजूद थे. किसी ने कहा "हम नहीं लेते मुसलमरान (मुसलमान) की जूठी औरत """ और यह आवाज़ रसालू, नेकीराम और चौकी कलाँ के बूढ़े मुहर्रिर के नारों में गुम होकर रह गई। इन सब आवाज़ों से अलग कालका प्रशाद की फटती और चिल्लाती आवाज़ आ रही थी. वह खाँस भी लेता और बोलता भी जाता। वह इस नई हकीकत, इस नई शुद्धि का शिद्दत से कायल हो चुका था। यूँ मालूम होता था आज इसने कोई नया वेद, कोई नया पुराण और शास्त्र पढ़ लिया है और अपने इस हुसूल' में दूसरों को भी हिस्सेदार बनाना चाहता है इन सब लोगों और इनकी आवाज़ों में घिरे हुए लाजो और सुंदरलाल अपने डेरे को जा रहे थे और ऐसा जान पड़ता था, जैसे हज़ारों साल पहले के रामचंद्र और सीता किसी बहुत लंबे इखलाकी बनवास के बाद अयोध्या लौट रहे हैं। एक तरफ तो लोग खुशी के इज़हार में दीपमाला कर रहे हैं और दूसरी तरफ उन्हें इतनी लंबी अज़ीयत' दिए जाने पर तास्सुफ भी। लाजवंती के चले आने पर भी सुंदरलाल बाबू ने इसी शिद्दत से 'दिल में बसाओ' प्रोग्राम को जारी रखा। उसने कौल और फेल' दोनों एतबार से उसे निभा दिया था और वह लोग, जिन्हें सुंदरलाल की बातों में खाली-खुली जज़्बातियत' नज़र आती थी, कायल होना शुरू हुए। अकसर लोगों के दिल में खुशी थी और बेशतर के दिल में अफ़सोस । मकान 414 की बेवा के अलावा मुहल्ला मुल्ला शकूर की बहुत सी औरतें सुंदरलाल बाबू सोशल वर्कर के घर आने से घबराती थीं। लेकिन सुंदरलाल को किसी की एतना" या बेएतनाई'' की परवा न थी। उसके दिल की रानी आ चुकी थी और उसके दिल का खिला' पट चुका था। सुंदरलाल ने लाजो की स्वर्ण-मूर्ति को अपने दिल के मंदिर में स्थापित कर लिया था और खुद दरवाज़े पर बैठा उसकी हिफाज़त करने लगा था। लाज़ो जो पहले ख़ौफ़ से सहमी रहती थी, सुंदरलाल के गैरमुतवक्का नर्म सुलूक को देखकर आहिस्ता आहिस्ता खुलने लगी। सुंदरलाल लाजवंती को अब लाजो के नाम से नहीं पुकारता था, वह उसे कहता था : "देवी !” और लाजो एक अनजान खुशी से पागल हुई जाती थी। वह कितना चाहती थी कि सुंदरलाल को अपनी वारदात कह सुनाए और सुनाते-सुनाते इस कदर रोए कि उसके सब गुनाह धुल जाएँ। लेकिन सुंदरलाल लाजो की वह बातें सुनने से गुरेज़ करता था और लाजो अपने खुल जाने में भी एक तरह से सिमटी रहती। अलबत्ता जब सुंदरलाल सो जाता तो उसे देखा ann.translation: Committees were formed in every street and every neighborhood, and at first, they diligently started the program of 'resettlement' in business, 'resettlement' on land, and 'resettlement' in homes. But there was one program that no one paid attention to. That program was about abducted women, and its slogan was 'resettle them in hearts'. This program faced strong opposition from Narayan Bawa's temple and the conservative communities living around it. To put this program into action, a committee was established in the Mullah Shakur neighborhood near the temple, and Sundarlal Babu was elected its secretary by a majority of eleven votes. The lawyer sahib, the head of Chowki Kalan, and the old clerk, and other respected people of the neighborhood, thought that no one else could do that work with more dedication than Sundarlal. ann.translation: Bedi had completely immersed himself in public service. Despite this, joining in with the voices of his other companions, he certainly used to get the thought that the human heart is so delicate. It can be hurt by even a small thing. It is like the touch-me-not plant, which wilts even if you just extend your hand towards it. But he left no stone unturned in mistreating his Lajwanti. He used to beat her for sitting and standing in inappropriate places, for being careless about eating, and for other such trivial matters. And Lajo was a delicate village girl, like a thin mulberry branch. Due to seeing too much sun, her complexion had become dark. There was a strange restlessness in her nature. Her agitation was like that drop of dew that rolls here and there on a large leaf of the mercury plant. Her thinness was not a sign of her poor health; it was a sign of a healthy body. Seeing this, the heavy-set Sundarlal was initially scared, but when he saw that Lajo could endure every kind of burden, every kind of shock, even beatings, he gradually increased his mistreatment and did not even consider the limits beyond which any human's patience can break. In blurring these boundaries, Lajwanti herself also proved helpful. Since she couldn't stay sad for long, even after the biggest fight, just one smile from Sunderlal would make her unable to stop her laughter, and she would rush to him, put her arms around his neck, and exclaim, "If you hit me again, I won't speak to you!" It was clear that she had completely forgotten all the beating. Like other girls in the village, she also knew that men behave this way. In fact, if any woman showed defiance, the girls themselves would put a finger to their nose and say, "Is that even a man, if a woman doesn't come under his control?" And this beating had made its way into their songs. Lajjo herself used to sing, "I won't marry a city boy, he wears boots, and my waist is very thin." But at the first opportunity, Lajjo fell in love with a city boy, and his name was Sunderlal, who had come to Lajwanti's village with a wedding procession and who had only whispered this much into the groom's ear: "Your sister-in-law is so 'salty', friend! Your wife must be 'spicy' too!" Lajwanti had heard Sundarlal's comment, but she completely forgot how big and ugly Sundarlal's boots were and how thin her own waist was.

ann.translation: So, to implement the 'Embrace in your heart' program, this committee of neighborhood Mullah Shakur organized several morning processions. Four or five in the morning was the most opportune time for them. There was no noise from people, no traffic congestion. Even the dogs, who had been on guard duty all night, would be lying with their heads buried in extinguished ovens. People, huddled in their beds, would hear the voices of the morning procession participants and just say, "Oh, it's that same group again!" And then, sometimes with patience and sometimes with irritation, they would listen to Babu Sundarlal's propaganda. Those women who had safely reached the other side would lie spread out like cauliflower florets, and their husbands, stiff like stalks beside them, would protest the noise of the morning procession, muttering something under their breath as they went along. Or somewhere, a child would open their eyes for a little while, and understanding the 'Embrace in your heart' program's plaintive and sorrowful propaganda as just a song, would fall back asleep.

ann.translation: But a word heard in the morning does not go to waste. It keeps spinning in the mind all day long, like an argument, and sometimes a person doesn't even understand its meaning, but keeps humming it. It was due to this voice taking root that in those days, when Miss Mridula Sarabhai brought back abducted women in exchange between India and Pakistan, some men from Mullah Shakur's neighborhood were ready to resettle them. Their heirs went to meet them at Chowki Kalan, outside the city. ann.translation: In vain, Bedi was hitting the ground with his stick and making a mournful sound, and somewhere among them, Sunderlal was going, tears still flowing from his eyes. Today, his heart was deeply hurt, and people were singing together with great enthusiasm: "Hath laaiyaan kumhlaani lajavanti de boote." The sound of the song was still echoing in people's ears. It wasn't even morning yet, and the widow of Mullah Shakur's house in the neighborhood was still taking painful stretches in her bed when Sunderlal's neighbor Lalchand, whom Sunderlal and Khalifa Kalka Prasad had given a ration depot by using their influence, came running and, spreading his hands from his thick sheet, said, "Congratulations, Sunderlal!" Sunderlal, while putting sweet tobacco in the chillum, said, "Congratulations for what, Lalchand?" "I saw Lajo Bhabhi!" The chillum fell from Sunderlal's hand, and the sweet tobacco scattered on the floor. "Where did you see her?" He grabbed Lalchand by the shoulders and asked, and not getting an answer quickly, he shook him. Sundarlal let go of Lalchand at the Wagah border and said only this much, "It must be someone else." Lalchand reassured him, "No, brother, it was Lajjo herself. Lajjo! You even recognize her!" Sundarlal again picked up the sweet tobacco from the floor, rubbed it in his palm, and asked, doing so, he picked up Risalo's chillum from the hookah and said, "What is her identification?" "One tattoo is on her chin, another on her cheek." "Yes, yes, yes!" And Sundarlal himself said, "The third is on her forehead." He didn't want any doubt to remain now, and suddenly he remembered all the familiar tattoos on Lajwanti's body, which she had gotten made on her body in childhood, which were like those light green seeds that are on the body of a touch-me-not plant, and which, as soon as you point to it, begins to wither. In exactly the same way, as soon as a finger was pointed at these tattoos, Lajwanti would become shy and disappear, as if all her secrets had become known to someone, and as if she had become impoverished by the looting of some unknown treasure. Sundarlal's whole body began to be thrown into an unknown fear, an unknown love, and its sacred fire. He again grabbed Lalchand and asked, "How did Lajo reach Wagah?" ann.translation: Then what happened? Sundarlal, squatting, said, "What happened then?" Rasalu also sat up on his cot and, coughing the characteristic cough of tobacco users, said, "Has Lajwanti Bhabhi really come?" Lalchand, continuing his story, said, "At Wagah, Pakistan gave sixteen women, and in exchange, took sixteen women. But a dispute arose. Our volunteers were objecting that the women you gave are mostly middle-aged, old, and useless women. People gathered over this dispute. At that time, the volunteers from that side, showing Lajo Bhabhi, said, 'You call her old? Look, look, does even one of the women you gave compare to her?' And there, Lajo Bhabhi was hiding her tattoos from everyone's eyes. Then the dispute escalated. Both sides decided to take back their respective 'goods'. I shouted, 'Lajo, Lajo Bhabhi!' but the soldiers of our nation beat us and chased us away. And Lalchand began to show his elbow where he had been hit by a stick. Rasalu and Nekiram remained silent, and Sunderlal started looking far away. Perhaps he began to think, "Lajo came, but didn't come." And from Sunderlal's face, it seemed as if he had crossed the desert of Bikaner and was now panting with his tongue out in the shade of some tree. He couldn't even manage to say, "Give him water." He felt that the violence of before and after the Partition was still effective, only its form had changed. Now people no longer had the same hesitation as before. If you ask anyone, "Did Lehna Singh live in Sambharwala, and his sister-in-law Banto?" they would immediately say, "They died." And after that, completely unaware of death and its meaning, completely indifferent, they would move on. Going one step further than this, with a very cold heart, human traders began to trade human goods, human flesh and skin, and exchange them. Cattle buyers used to open the jaw of a buffalo or cow and estimate its age from its teeth. Now, they started openly displaying the youth of a young woman, her glow, her most intimate secrets, her 'tandols'. Cruelty had now permeated the very being of these traders. Earlier, goods were sold in the market, and bargainers would shake hands, throw a handkerchief over them, and secretly make a deal as if the transaction was done with finger gestures under the handkerchief. Now, even the handkerchief for secret deals was gone, and transactions were happening openly, and people had forgotten the etiquette of trade. This whole transaction, this business, seemed like an old tale in which the story of the free buying and selling of women is narrated. Az-bayak stands before countless naked women, examining their bodies by touching them. And when he touches a woman's body with his finger, a pink mark appears on it, and around it, a pale circle, and then paleness and redness race to take each other's place. Az-bayak moves on, and the unacceptable woman, in a state of defeat and humiliation, holds her drawstring with one hand and hides her face from the public's gaze with the other, sobbing.

ann.translation: Sundarlal was just preparing to go to Amritsar border when he received news of Lajo's arrival. Sundarlal was immediately flustered by such news. His foot immediately moved towards the door, but he turned back. He wanted to get angry and sit down spreading all the committee's placards and flags, and then cry. But there, such a display of emotions was not possible. He manly faced this inner struggle and, measuring his steps, walked towards Chowki Kalan, because that was the place where the abducted women were delivered. Now Lajo stood before him, trembling with a feeling of fear. Only she knew Sundarlal. No one else knew. He used to treat her like that even before, and now that she had come after spending days of her life with another man, who knows what he would do. Sundarlal looked at Lajo. She was wearing a purely Islamic-style red dupatta and had her veil drawn on the left side. It was merely out of habit, a habit of blending in with other women and ultimately having the ease of escaping her captor's snare. And she was thinking so much about Sunderlal that she didn't even think of changing her clothes or adjusting her dupatta properly. She was unable to distinguish between the fundamental differences of Hindu and Muslim culture, between a right-side veil and a left-side veil. Now she stood before Sunderlal, trembling with a feeling of both hope and fear. Sunderlal felt a jolt. He saw that Lajwanti's complexion had brightened somewhat, and she looked a bit healthier than before. No, she had gotten fat. Everything Sunderlal had imagined about Lajo was wrong. He thought that after dissolving in sorrow, Lajwanti would have become completely emaciated, and her voice would not come out of her mouth. He was greatly shocked by the thought that she had been very happy in Pakistan, but he remained silent because he had sworn to remain silent. Although he couldn't understand that if she was so happy, then why did she come back? He thought that perhaps due to the pressure of the Indian government, she had to come here against her will. But there was one thing he couldn't understand: Lajwanti's darkened face was tinged with yellowness, and due to sheer sorrow, the flesh of her body had left her bones. She had become fat from an excess of sorrow and appeared healthy. But this was such a health that after walking two steps, a person would lose their breath. Upon casting the first glance at Mughviya's face, the impression was somewhat strange, but he confronted all thoughts with a resolute manliness. Many other people were also present. Someone said, "We do not take the leavings of a Muslim woman." And this voice was lost in the slogans of Rasalu, Nekiram, and the old clerk of Chauki Kalan. Separate from all these voices, Kalka Prasad's cracking and shouting voice was coming. He would cough and also keep speaking. He had become intensely convinced of this new reality, this new purification. It seemed as if today he had read some new Veda, some new Purana, and some new Shastra, and in this achievement of his, he wanted to make others partners too. Surrounded by all these people and their voices, Lajo and Sundarlal were going to their dwelling. And it seemed as if Ramchandra and Sita of thousands of years ago were returning to Ayodhya after a very long moral exile. On one hand, people were celebrating with rows of lamps in expression of joy, and on the other hand, there was regret over them being subjected to such a long torment. Even after Lajwanti's departure, Sundarlal Babu had continued the 'Basaao' program with the same intensity. He had fulfilled it both in word and deed. And those people who saw only empty sentimentality in Sundarlal's words began to be convinced. Often, there was happiness in people's hearts, and mostly, there was regret in their hearts. Besides the widow of the house, many women from Mullah Shakur's neighborhood were hesitant to come to Social Worker Sunderlal's house. But Sunderlal didn't care about anyone's attention or inattention. The queen of his heart had arrived, and the lotus of his heart had bloomed. Sunderlal had enshrined Lajo's golden idol in the temple of his heart, and he himself sat at the door, guarding it. Lajo, who used to remain timid with fear, slowly began to open up after seeing Sunderlal's unexpected gentle behavior. Sunderlal no longer called Lajwanti by the name Lajo. He called her "Devi," and Lajo would go mad with an unknown joy. How much she wanted to tell Sunderlal her story and cry so much while telling it that all her sins would be washed away. ann.translation: If he asked the reason, she would say nothing but "Ooh-hoo" and the tired Sundarlal would doze off again. However, once in the very beginning, Sundarlal had only asked this much about Lajwanti's dark days: "Who was he?" Lajwanti lowered her gaze and said, "Jamal." Then she wanted to say something, fixing her gaze on Sundarlal's face, but Sundarlal was looking at Lajwanti's face with a strange look and stroking her hair. Lajwanti again lowered her eyes, and Sundarlal asked, "Did he treat you well?" "Yes." "He didn't hit you, did he?" Lajwanti, sliding her head onto Sundarlal's chest, said, "No." And then she spoke, "He didn't hit me, but I was more afraid of him. You used to hit me too, but I wasn't afraid of you. Now you won't hit me, will you?" Tears welled up in Sundarlal's eyes, and he said with great regret and remorse, "No, Devi." “No, no, I won't hit you,” Sundarlal said. Lajwanti thought, and she too began to cry. And after that, Lajwanti wanted to tell everything, but Sundarlal said, “Let bygones be bygones. What fault is yours in this? The fault lies with our society, which does not give respect to goddesses like you in its midst. It does not harm you, it harms itself.” And Lajwanti's thoughts remained in her mind. She could not say everything and remained quiet and subdued, looking at her body, which after the partition had now become the body of a goddess, not Lajwanti's. She was happy, very happy, but immersed in such happiness that contained doubt and apprehension. She would suddenly sit up while lying down, as if, in moments of extreme happiness, hearing a sound, she would suddenly become attentive to it. When many days passed, doubt completely took the place of happiness. Not because Sundarlal Babu had started his old mistreatment again, but because he had started treating Lajo very well. Such treatment, which Lajo did not expect. She wanted to be the old Lajo who would fight over a carrot and be appeased by a radish. But now there was no question of a fight. Sunderlal had made her feel as if she was a glass object that would break with a touch. And Lajo would look at her reflection in the mirror and finally come to the conclusion that she could be everything else, but not Lajo. She was settled but ruined. Sunderlal had no eyes to see her tears, nor ears to hear her sighs. Morning processions kept coming out, and the neighborhood Mullah Shakoor, along with reformer Rasalu and Nekiram, kept singing in the same voice: 'The hands that brought the plants have withered, Lajo, the plants.'

रंगना.etym: From रंग (raṅg, “color”) + -ना (-nā). Compare Gujarati રંગવું (raṅgvũ), Marathi रंगणे (raṅgṇe), Sindhi رڱڻ (rṅṇ) / रङणु, Punjabi ਰੰਗਣਾ (raṅgṇā) / رَنگݨا (rangṇā).

तबीयत.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian طبیعت (tabī'at), from Arabic طَبِيعَة (ṭabīʕa). Compare Bengali তবিয়ত (tobiẏot), Gujarati તબિયત (tabiyat), Punjabi ਤਬੀਅਤ (tabīata).

अजीब.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian عجیب ('ajīb), from Arabic عَجِيب (ʕajīb).

बेकारी.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بیکَارِی (bēkārī). By surface analysis, बे- (be-) + कार (kār) + -ई (-ī) (बेकार (bekār) + -ई (-ī) and/or बे- (be-) + कारी (kārī)).

उधर.etym: Connected with धार (dhār, “flow, stream”), which means "direction" in Old Hindi or Braj Bhasha. For the u- prefix, compare उस (us, “that”) and उतना (utnā, “this much”).

सेहत.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian صحت (sihhat), from Arabic صِحَّة (ṣiḥḥa). Compare Punjabi ਸਿਹਤ (sihat).

खराब.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian خراب (xarāb), from Arabic خَرَاب (ḵarāb). Compare Bengali খারাব (kharab), Nepali खराब (kharāb), Punjabi ਖ਼ਰਾਬ (xarāb), Tulu ಖರಾಬ್ (kharābŭ).

दलील.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian دلیل (dalīl), from Arabic دَلِيل (dalīl). Compare Bengali দলিল (dolil).

किस्म.etym: Borrowed from Arabic قِسْم (qism, “portion, section”). Compare Bengali কিসিম (kisim), Punjabi ਕ਼ਿਸਮ (qisam).

बोझ.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀯𑁄𑀚𑁆𑀛 (vojjha), from Sanskrit वह्य (vahya), from Proto-Indo-European *wóǵʰ-yo-s (“fit to be carried”), from *weǵʰ- (“to carry, draw”).

हद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian حدّ (hadd), from Arabic حَدّ (ḥadd). Compare Bengali হদ্দ (hoddo), Gujarati હદ (had), Marathi हद्द (hadda), Punjabi ਹੱਦ (hadda) / حد (hadd).

जहाँ.etym: Invented as a co-ordinate term for यहाँ (yahā̃, “here”), from Sanskrit इह (ihá).

पहुँचना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀧𑀳𑀼𑀘𑁆𑀘𑀇 (pahuccaï, “to reach, be powerful”); see there for more.

बाद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بعد (ba'd), from Arabic بَعْد (baʕd).

इनसान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian اِنْسَان (insān), borrowed from Arabic إِنْسَان (ʔinsān), from Proto-Semitic *ʔināš- (“man, person”).

सब्र.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian صَبْر (sabr), from Arabic صَبْر (ṣabr). Compare Bengali সবর (śobor).

कान.etym: Inherited from Apabhramsa 𑖎𑖜𑖿𑖜 (kaṇṇa), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀓𑀡𑁆𑀡 (kaṇṇa), from Sanskrit कर्ण (karṇa, “ear”). Doublet of कर्ण (karṇ).

इतना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀇𑀢𑁆𑀢𑀺𑀦 (*ittina), 𑀇𑀢𑁆𑀢𑀺𑀮 (ittila), ultimately from Sanskrit इयत्तक (iyattaká). Cognate with Punjabi ਇੰਨਾ (innā), Gujarati એટલું (eṭalũ), Marathi इतके (itke).

कहा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀓𑀳𑀸 (kahā), from Sanskrit कथा (kathā).

सालना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀲𑀮𑁆𑀮𑀺𑀅 (sallia), from Sanskrit शाल्ययति (śālyayati).

साला.etym: The mildly vulgar senses imply that the speaker is having sexual relations with the offended person's sister, although this connotation is now obscure and rarely implied.

नमकीन.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian نَمَکِین (namakīn). By surface analysis, नमक (namak, “salt”) + -ईन (-īn).

यार.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian یار (yār). Compare Gujarati યાર (yār), Punjabi ਯਾਰ (yār), Marwari यार (yār).

senses.gloss: to take abuse passively, to bear, suffer silently

सुनना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit सुणइ (suṇaï), from Sanskrit शृणोति (śṛṇoti), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćr̥náwti, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱl̥néwti. Cognate with Nepali सुन्नु (sunnu) and Assamese শুনা (xuna), and distantly with Irish cluin (“to hear”).

मगर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مگر (magar). Compare Bengali মাগার (magar), Punjabi ਮਗਰ (magar).
Inherited from Prakrit मगर (magara), from Sanskrit मकर (mákara).

भद्दा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀪𑀤𑁆𑀤 (bhadda, “fortunate”), from Sanskrit भद्र (bhadra, “fortunate, delightful”), per Turner.

senses.gloss: at the time that, when (after the imperfective participle ते)

समय.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit स॒म॒य (samayá). Doublet of समाँ (samā̃) and समै (samai).
Learned borrowing from Sanskrit स॒म॒य (samayá). Doublet of समाँ (samā̃) and समै (samai).

senses.gloss: a male given name, Samay, from Sanskrit

समय.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit स॒म॒य (samayá). Doublet of समाँ (samā̃) and समै (samai).

याद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian یاد (yād), from Middle Persian. Compare Bengali ইয়াদ (iẏad).

जाया.etym: Inherited from Prakrit जाय (jāya), from Sanskrit जात (jāta). Cognate with Gujarati જાયું (jāyũ) and very distantly to English né.
Inherited from Prakrit जाय (jāya), from Sanskrit जात (jāta). Cognate with Gujarati જાયું (jāyũ) and very distantly to English né.

बिचारा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بیچاره (bēčāra, “poor, helpless, pathetic”), from بی (bē, “without”) + چاره (čāra, “help”). Compare Punjabi ਵਿਚਾਰਾ (vicārā) / وِچارا (vicārā), Gujarati બિચારું (bicārũ), Marathi बिचारे (bicāre), Bengali বেচারা (becara), Assamese বেচেৰা (besera).

शिकार.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian شکار (šikār). Compare Assamese চিকাৰ (sikar), Bengali শিকার (śikar), Gujarati શિકાર (śikār), Odia ଶିକାର (śikāra).

ग़लती.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian غَلَطِی (ġalatī), ultimately from Arabic غَلَط (ḡalaṭ). By surface analysis, ग़लत (ġalat) + -ई (-ī).

सहायक.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit सहायक (sahāyaka), equivalent to सहाय (sahāy, “helping, helper”) + -अक (-ak). Cognate with Marathi सहाय्यक (sahāyyak).
Borrowed from Sanskrit सहायक (sahāyaka), equivalent to सहाय (sahāy, “helping, helper”) + -अक (-ak). Cognate with Marathi सहाय्यक (sahāyyak).

मासूम.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مَعْصُوم (ma'sūm), from Arabic مَعْصُوم (maʕṣūm, “protected”), from root ع ص م (ʕ ṣ m). Compare Turkish masum.

अपनाना.etym: From अपना (apnā, “oneself”) + -आना (-ānā). Cognate with Gujarati અપનાવવું (apanāvvũ, “to adopt”).

ख़त्म.etym: Borrowed from Arabic خَتْم (ḵatm), verbal noun of خَتَمَ (ḵatama, “to end”). Compare Bengali খৎম (khotm), Punjabi ਖ਼ਤਮ (xatam), Gujarati ખતમ (khatam), Odia ଖତମ (khatama).

चाहना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀘𑀸𑀳𑀇 (cāhaï), possibly from Sanskrit काङ्क्षति (kāṅkṣati) or चक्ष॑ते (cákṣate).

आबाद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian آباد (ābād). Compare Punjabi ਅਬਾਦ (abād).

मर्तबा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مرتبه (martaba), from Arabic مَرْتَبَة (martaba, “status, degree, place, division”).

senses.gloss: a female given name, Prerna, from Sanskrit

माँ.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀫𑀸𑀤𑀸 (mādā), from Sanskrit मातृ (mātṛ, “mother”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *máHtā, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Doublet of माता (mātā), a tatsama. Compare Punjabi ਮਾਂ (mā̃), Gujarati મા (mā), માં (mā̃), Bengali মা (ma), Assamese মা (ma), O…

senses.gloss: sister (a female sibling of any age)

बहन.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀪𑀇𑀡𑀻 (bhaïṇī), 𑀪𑀕𑀺𑀡𑀻 (bhagiṇī), from Sanskrit भगिनी (bhaginī).

इशारा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian اشاره (išāra), from Arabic إِشَارَة (ʔišāra, “sign, signal”). Compare Punjabi ਇਸ਼ਾਰਾ (iśārā) / اِشارَہ (īśārah), Gujarati ઇશારો (iśāro), Marathi इशारा (iśārā), Bengali ইশারা (iśara).

senses.gloss: to put in possession (of), to occasion

दिलाना.etym: Causative form of देना (denā) with the suffix -लाना (-lānā).

छूना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀙𑀼𑀯𑀇 (chuvaï). Cognate with Punjabi ਛੂਹਣਾ (chūhṇā) / چھوہنا (chūhṇā).

मुआ.etym: Inherited from Prakrit मुअ (mua), मुद (muda) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-), from Sanskrit मृत (mṛta). Doublet of मुरदा (murdā), मृत (mŕt), and मरा (marā). Compare Gujarati મૂઉં (mūũ), Kachchi મુઓ (muo), Marathi मेले (mele).

senses.gloss: As you (or as one) would say

अमल.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit अमल (amala). By surface analysis, अ- (a-) + मल (mal).
Borrowed from Classical Persian عمل ('amal), from Arabic عَمَل (ʕamal).

जामा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جامه (jāma). Compare Bengali জামা (jama), Punjabi ਜਾਮਾ (jāmā).

पहनाना.etym: Causative form of पहनना (pahannā) with the suffix -आना (-ānā).

कई.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit [Term?], from Sanskrit कतिपय (katipaya, “several”), from कति (kati).
Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit [Term?], from Sanskrit कतिपय (katipaya, “several”), from कति (kati).

बजना.etym: From earlier बाजना (bājnā), from Prakrit वज्जइ (vajjaï), from Sanskrit वाद्यते (vādyate), the passive form of वादयति (vādayati), from the root वद् (vad, “to speak”). Compare Nepali बज्नु (bajnu), Gujarati વાગવું (vāgvũ), Marathi वाजणे (vāj̈ṇe), Assamese বাজা (baza), Sinhalese …

वक्त.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian وَقْت (waqt), from Arabic وَقْت (waqt). Compare Bengali ওয়াক্ত (ōẇakto), Punjabi ਵਕਤ (vakat), Santali ᱚᱠᱛᱚ (ôktô).

वक़्त.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian وَقْت (waqt), from Arabic وَقْت (waqt). Compare Bengali ওয়াক্ত (ōẇakto), Punjabi ਵਕਤ (vakat), Santali ᱚᱠᱛᱚ (ôktô).

शोर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian شور (šōr), from Old Persian [script needed] (xšar). Compare with Sanskrit अक्षरा (akṣarā, “word, speech”), root क्षर् (kṣar, “to flow, melt, perish”).

कुत्ता.etym: Inherited from Prakrit कुत्त (kutta) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-) without cluster simplification.

senses.gloss: to be extinguished (as of a fire, light)
to be cooled, slaked (as of hot iron, lime)
to be relieved (as of hunger, thirst)
to be calmed (as of agitated feelings)
to be dampened (as of ardour, morale)
to be subdued (as of the emotions or the voice)

तनूर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian تنور (tan(n)ūr), from Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (tnwl). Ultimately from Akkadian 𒋾𒂟 (tinūru). Compare Bengali তন্দুর (tondur), Punjabi ਤੰਦੂਰ (tandūr).

senses.gloss: one of the four top-valued playing cards

सर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian سر (sar). Cognate with Sanskrit शिरस् (śiras). Doublet of सिर (sir, “head”) and सिरा (sirā, “beginning”).

senses.gloss: to move ahead, proceed, to go ahead smoothly (a task, etc)
to be passed, or lived (time, life)

सरना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit सरइ (saraï, “moves, slips aside”), from Sanskrit सरति (sárati), a later thematic present verb of the root सृ (sṛ)—compare सिस॑र्ति॒ (sísarti, “runs”). Related to सरकना (saraknā), सरसराना (sarsarānā), पसरना (pasarnā).

senses.gloss: to fall, to fall down, to drop
to fall to the lot; to become one's assigned task or responsibility
to be met with, found (indicating spatial localization)

पड़ना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀧𑀟𑀇 (paḍaï), from Sanskrit पत॑ति (pátati), from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti, from *peth₂-. Compare Punjabi ਪੈਣਾ (paiṇā), Nepali पर्नु (parnu), Gujarati પડવું (paḍvũ), Bengali পড়া (poṛa), Assamese পৰা (pora). False cognate of Tamil படு (paṭu), Telugu ప…

बिस्तर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بستر (bistar). Compare with Sanskrit विस्तर (vistara, “layer, bed; anything spread out”).

senses.gloss: a small circle, disc, ring, or coil

मंडली.etym: मंडल (maṇḍal) + -ई (-ī). Compare Prakrit मंडल (maṃḍala, “group, circle”) and Sanskrit मण्डलिका (maṇḍalikā, “group”). Cognate with Bengali মণ্ডলী (monḍoli, “congregation”).

पार.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀸𑀭 (pāra), from Sanskrit पार (pāra).
Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀸𑀭 (pāra), from Sanskrit पार (pāra).

गोभी.etym: Some believe a derivative from Sanskrit गोजीह्विका (gojīhvikā), but it is unlikely.

फूल.etym: Cognates include Assamese ফুল (phul), Bengali ফুল (phul), Bhojpuri फूल (phūl), Gujarati ફૂલ (phūl), Maithili फूल (phūl), Marathi फूल (phūl), Nepali फूल (phūl), Odia ଫୁଲ (phula), Punjabi پھل / ਫੁੱਲ (phulla), and Sindhi ڦل (phulu).

फैलना.etym: Derived from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀥𑀺𑀤 (padhida) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀮𑁆𑀮- (-lla-), from Sanskrit प्रथित (prathita, “spread out”), from प्रथ् (prath), from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Marathi फैलावणे (phailāvṇe), Gujarati ફેલાવું (phelāvũ), Punjabi ਫੈਲਾਣਾ …

डंठल.etym: From Sanskrit *डण्ठ (*ḍaṇṭha, “stem”), possible diminutive तण्डक (taṇḍaka, “trunk”), related दण्ड (daṇḍá, “stick, club”), ultimately of non-Indo-Aryan origin.

senses.gloss: to insist, defy (to hold up a claim or idea stubbornly)

अकड़ना.etym: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *आकड्डइ (ākaḍḍaï). Cognate to Gujarati અકડાવું (akaḍāvũ), Marathi अकडणे (akaḍṇe). Possibly related to Hindi अँकड़ाना (ãkṛānā, “to cause to curl”).

मुँह.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀫𑀼𑀳 (muha), from Sanskrit मुख॑ (múkha), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *múkʰam, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *múkʰam, from *múkHam. Doublet of मुख (mukh), a tatsama.

senses.gloss: some, much, a bit of (with uncountable nouns)
some, much, a bit of (with uncountable nouns): not much
a few, some (not particularized): few, not many

कुछ.etym: From Old Hindi कछु (kachu) undergoing regular metathesis, somehow related to Prakrit किंचि n (kiṃci), कोइ m (koi), काइ f (kāi); see there for more. Related to कोई (koī), किसी (kisī), किन्हीं (kinhī̃). Cognate with Bengali কিছু (kichu) and Punjabi ਕੁਝ (kujh).

कहीं.etym: Blend of कहाँ (kahā̃, “where”) + ही (hī, emphatic particle).

बच्चा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بَچَّه (bačča), from Proto-Iranian *wacáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *watsás, from Proto-Indo-European *wetsós, from *wétos + *-ós. Doublet of बछड़ा (bachṛā, “calf, child, boy”).

थोड़ा.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi थोडा (thoḍā), from Prakrit थोअ (thoa) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀟- (-ḍa-) + -𑀓- (-ka-), from older थोव (thova), थोग (thoga), थोक (thoka), from Sanskrit स्तो॒क (stoká, “a drop”). Cognate with Punjabi ਥੋੜਾ (thoṛā), Gujarati થોડું (thoḍũ), Marathi थोडे (thoḍe)…

आँख.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀅𑀓𑁆𑀔𑀺 (akkhi), from Sanskrit अक्षि (akṣi), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Compare Pali akkhi, Romani jakh, Punjabi ਅੱਖ (akkha), Assamese আখি (akhi, “eye; a knot on a bamboo”). Cognate with English eye.

खोलना.etym: From Proto-New Indo-Aryan *खोल्लइ (khŏllaï) of uncertain origin. See there for more. Cognate with Bengali খোলা (khōla), Gujarati ખોલવું (kholvũ), and Nepali खोल्नु (kholnu).

समझ.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑀁𑀩𑀼𑀚𑁆𑀛 (saṃbujjha). By surface analysis, deverbal form of समझना (samajhnā). Cognate with Marathi समज (samaj).

समझना.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi समझना (samajhanā), समुझना (samujhanā), from Prakrit संबुज्झइ (saṃbujjhaï), संबुज्झदि (saṃbujjhadi), from Sanskrit सम्बुध्यते (sambudhyate). Cognate with Punjabi ਸਮਝਣਾ (samjhaṇā) / سَمجھݨا (samjhṇā), Gujarati સમજવું (samajvũ), Marathi समजणे (samajṇe). C…

सो.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑁄 (so), from Sanskrit स (sa, third person singular pronoun). Cognate with Old Awadhi सो (so), Punjabi ਸੋ (so), Marwari सो (so), Bihari सो, Nepali सो (so). Also see तिस (tis).

सोना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit सोअइ (soaï, “sleeps”). See there for more. Related to सुतना (sutnā, “to sleep”) and सपना (sapnā, “dream”). Cognate with Bengali শোয়া (śōẇa), Odia ସୋଇବା (soibā), Punjabi ਸੌਣਾ (sauṇā), and Romani sovel.

शब्द.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit शब्द (śabda). Doublet of साद (sād).

senses.gloss: day (period from one midnight to the next)
day, daytime (period between sunrise and sunset)

दिन.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi दिन (dina), from Prakrit दिण (diṇa), from Sanskrit दिन (dina), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *dinám, from Proto-Indo-European *di-nó- (“day”), from the root *dyew- (“to shine”). Cognate with Bengali দিন (din), Nepali दिन (dina), and more distantly with Russi…

तकरार.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian تَکْرَار (takrār), from Arabic تَكْرَار (takrār, “repetition, reiteration, frequency”); compare Tamil தகராறு (takarāṟu), Tulu ತಕ್ರಾರು (takrāru).

दिमाग़.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian دِمَاغ (dimāġ), borrowed from Arabic دِمَاغ (dimāḡ), a blend of دَم (dam) + مُخّ (muḵḵ).

चक्कर.etym: Semi-learned borrowing from Sanskrit चक्र (cakra). Doublet of चाक (cāk), चक्का (cakkā), चक्र (cakra), and चरख़ा (carxā). Cognate with Punjabi ਚੱਕਰ (cakkar), Bengali চক্কর (cokkor), Assamese চকৰ (sokor) and চকৰি (sokori), Sylheti ꠌꠇꠞ (soxor).

बाज़.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian باز (bāz). Compare Bengali বাজ (baj), Punjabi ਬਾਜ਼ (bāz).

मानी.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian معنی (ma'nī), from Arabic مَعْنَى (maʕnā). Compare Assamese মানে (mane), Bengali মানে (mane).

मानना.etym: Gujarati માનવું (mānvũ), Marathi मानणे (mānṇe), Bengali মানা (mana), Assamese মনা (mona) / মানা (mana).

गुनगुनाना.etym: Onomatopoeic reduplication. Compare Nepali गुनगुनाउनु (gunagunāunu), Marathi गुणगुणणे (guṇguṇṇe).

senses.gloss: emphatic of इस (is): only this, just this
a male given name, Mridul, from Sanskrit
the Indian subcontinent, India (a region of South Asia, traditionally delimited by the Himalayas and the Indus river; the Indian subcontinent)

हिंद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian هند (hind), from Middle Persian hnd (hind), from Old Persian 𐏃𐎡𐎯𐎢𐏁 (hiⁿdūš), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *sindʰus (“river”) or from Sanskrit सिन्धु (sindhu, “a river, stream”). Doublet of सिंध (sindh) and सिंधु (sindhu).

पाकिस्तान.etym: Borrowed from Urdu پاکِسْتان (pākistān). By surface analysis, पाक (pāk) + -इस्तान (-istān).

दरमियान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian درمیان (darmiyān). Compare Marathi दरम्यान (daramyān), Punjabi ਦਰਮਿਆਨ (darmiāna).
Borrowed from Classical Persian درمیان (darmiyān). Compare Marathi दरम्यान (daramyān), Punjabi ਦਰਮਿਆਨ (darmiāna).

तबादला.etym: Borrowed from Arabic تَبَادَلَ (tabādala) or a related word.

तैयार.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian تیار (tayyār), from Arabic طَيَّار (ṭayyār). Compare Gujarati તૈયાર (taiyār), Marathi तयार (tayār), Punjabi ਤਿਆਰ (tiāra), Malayalam തയ്യാർ (tayyāṟ), Tamil தயார் (tayār).

वारिस.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian وارث (wāris), from Arabic وَارِث (wāriṯ). Compare Bengali ওয়ারিস (ōẇariś), Gujarati વારસ (vāras), Marathi वारस (vāras), Punjabi ਵਾਰਸ (vāras).

बाहर.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀩𑀸𑀳𑀺𑀭 (bāhira), from Sanskrit बहिर् (bahir), a compounding form of बहिस् (bahis). Compare Marathi बाहेर (bāher), Assamese বাহিৰ (bahir).

सिर.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Apabhramsa सिरु (siru), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑀺𑀭 (sira), from Sanskrit शिरस् (śiras). Compare with Persian سر (sar) (from Middle Persian 𐭫𐭥𐭩𐭱𐭤 (sar)) and Avestan 𐬯𐬁𐬭𐬀 (sāra). Doublet of सर (sar, “head”) and सिरा (sirā, “beginning”).

बरबाद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian برباد (bar-bād, literally “to the wind”). Compare Punjabi ਬਰਬਾਦ (barbād), Bengali বরবাদ (borbad).

चल.etym: From Sanskrit चल (cala, “moving, trembling; unsteady, perishable; disturbed, confused”).

सिंह.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit सिंह (siṃha). Doublet of सिंघ (siṅgh).

सिंह.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit सिंह (siṃha). Doublet of सिंघ (siṅgh).

नारा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian نعره (na'ra), from Arabic نَعْرَة (naʕra).

सूखना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit सुक्खइ (sukkhaï, “to become dry”), a verbalization of सुक्ख (sukkha, “dry”), whence Hindi सूखा (sūkhā, “dry”). Cognate with Old Awadhi सूखइ (sūkhaï), Marathi सुकणे (sukṇe), Nepali सुक्नु (suknu), Punjabi ਸੁੱਕਣਾ (sukkaṇā), Odia ସୁଖିବା (sukhibā), and Gujar…

शौहर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian شوهر (šawhar), from Proto-Iranian *fšautar.

बाप.etym: Inherited from Apabhramsa बप्प (bappa), from Prakrit बप्प (bappa). Cognate with Assamese বাপ (bap), Bengali বাপ (bap), Odia ବାପା (bāpā), Punjabi ਬਾਪੂ /باپو (bāpū), Gujarati બાપ (bāp).

senses.gloss: used to refer to any male person

भाई.etym: Cognate with Punjabi ਭਰਾ (bharā) / بھرا (bharā), Sindhi भाऊ / ڀاءُ (bhāū), Gujarati ભાઈ (bhāī), Marathi भाऊ (bhāū), Bengali ভাই (bhai), Persian برادر (barâdar), Ancient Greek φράτηρ (phrátēr), Latin frāter, Old Norse bróðir and Old English brōþor (English brother).

senses.gloss: to recognize, to distinguish; to identify

पहचानना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit [Term?], from metathesis of Prakrit 𑀧𑀘𑁆𑀘𑀳𑀺𑀆𑀡𑀇 (paccahiāṇaï), from Sanskrit प्रत्यभिजानाति (pratyabhijānāti), from the root प्रत्यभिज्ञा (pratyabhijñā); compare the un-prefixed form of the verb, जानाति (jānāti), as well as a nominal derivation, …

इनकार.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian انکار (inkār), from Arabic إِنْكَار (ʔinkār).

आखिर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian آخِر (āxir), from Arabic آخِر (ʔāḵir).
Borrowed from Classical Persian آخِر (āxir), from Arabic آخِر (ʔāḵir).

मरना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀫𑀭𑀇 (maraï), from Sanskrit मर॑ति (márati). Cognate with Nepali मर्नु (marnu).

क्यों.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi क्यूं (kyūṃ), from Apabhramsa किंव (kiṃva), केंव (keṃva), from the interrogative base in क्- (k-) + एंव (eṃva), for which see यों (yõ).

बचाना.etym: Regular transitive form of बचना (bacnā). Cognate to Punjabi ਬਚਾਉਣਾ (bacāuṇā) / بَچاؤݨا (bacā'oṇā), Marathi वाचवणे (vāċavṇe).

ज़हर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian زهر (zahr). Compare Bengali জহর (johor), Gujarati ઝેર (jher).

senses.gloss: well (hole in the ground for fetching water)

कुआँ.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi कुआ (kuā), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀓𑀽𑀯𑀅 (kūvaa), 𑀓𑀽𑀯𑀕 (kūvaga), from Sanskrit कूपक (kūpaka) (see कूप (kūpa)), from Proto-Indo-European *kewp-. Doublet of कप (kap, “cup”).

छलाँगना.etym: Most likely from a derivative of Sanskrit लङ्घति (láṅghati, “to ascend”). Compare Hindi उछलना (uchalnā, “jump”), with similar prefix.

बुज़दिल.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بزدل (buz-dil), from بز (buz, “goat”) + دل (dil, “heart”).

senses.gloss: life (as in the state of being alive)

ज़िंदगी.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian زندگی (zindagī). Compare Bengali জিন্দেগি (jindegi), Punjabi ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀ (zindgī), Tamil ஜிந்தகி (jintaki, “property”).

senses.gloss: to cling to, hang on, embrace, hold fast

चिमटना.etym: Derived from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *चिंबइ (ciṃbaï) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀝𑁆𑀝- (-ṭṭa-). See also चिमटा (cimṭā).

जान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جان (jān), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian *wyaHnás, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe”). Cognate with Sanskrit व्यान (vyāna). Compare Assamese জান (zan), Bengali জান (jan), Punjabi ਜਾਨ (jān).

senses.gloss: outward appearance, form, figure, shape, appearance, semblance, image, representation, picture

विरोध.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit विरोध (virodha). By surface analysis, वि- (vi-) + रोध (rodh).

senses.gloss: relative (a family member, normally of the extended family)

रिश्तेदार.etym: Oblique of रिश्ता (riśtā, “relation”) + -दार (-dār, “bearing”). Compare Punjabi ਰਿਸ਼ਤੇਦਾਰ (riśtedār).

पवित्रता.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit पवित्रता (pavitratā). By surface analysis, पवित्र (pavitra) + -ता (-tā)

ज़िंदा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian زنده (zinda), from Middle Persian zyndk', zywndk' (zīndag, “alive”). Compare Bengali জিন্দা (jinda), Punjabi ਜਿੰਦਾ (jindā).

senses.gloss: what type of, what kind of

कैसा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Apabhramsa कइस (kaïsa), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀓𑀻𑀇𑀲 (kīisa), from Sanskrit कीदृश (kīdṛśa).

मौत.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian موت (mawt), from Arabic مَوْت (mawt). Compare Punjabi ਮੌਤ (maut).

घूर.etym: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *घूर (ghūra, “stare, frown”) of uncertain origin. Cognate with Punjabi ਘੂਰ /ਘੂਰ (ghūr), Sindhi [script needed] (ghūra) and probably related to Hindi घुड़कना (ghuṛaknā) / घुरकना (ghuraknā, “to frown at, frighten”).

घूरना.etym: From घूर (ghūr, “stare, frown”) + -ना (-nā). Compare Nepali घुरकनु (ghurakanu, “to frown”).

senses.gloss: the honorific particle, usually appended to names (of any gender) and titles

an expression of enquiry; yes?, who is it?

जी.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi जी (jī), from Prakrit 𑀚𑀻𑀅 (jīa), from Sanskrit जीव (jī́va, “long live”), the imperative of जीवति (jī́vati, “is alive”). Cognate with Braj जू (jū), Assamese জীউ (ziu).

senses.gloss: heart, mind (in the figurative, not anatomical, sense)

जी.etym: Inherited from Prakrit जीअ (jīa), जीव (jīva, “life, body, soul”), from Sanskrit जीव (jīvá, “alive”). Related to the etymology above. Cognate with Assamese জীউ (ziu), Nepali जीउ (jīu, “body”), Gujarati જીવ (jīv), and more distantly with English quick, French vif.

जीना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit जीवइ (jīvaï), from Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati). Cognate with French vivre and Russian жить (žitʹ).

दोहराना.etym: From दोहरा (dohrā, “double, reduplicated”). Compare Assamese দোহাৰ (dühar).

आखिरी.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian آخِرِی (āxirī), from آخِر (āxir) + ـِی (-ī).

तू.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Apabhramsa तुहुं (tuhuṃ), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀢𑀼𑀫𑀁 (tumaṃ), 𑀢𑀼𑀁 (tuṃ), from Sanskrit त्वम् (tvam), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *tuHám, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Doublet of तुस्सी (tussī).

गोदना.etym: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *गोद्दइ (gŏddaï) a variant form of *खोद्दइ (khŏddaï), whence खोदना (khodnā). See there for more.

खिलाना.etym: Causative form of खाना (khānā) with the suffix -लाना (-lānā).

चिल्लाना.etym: Related to किल्लाना (killānā), from Sanskrit किलकिलायति (kilakilāyati, “it cries, shrieks”), ultimately onomatopoeic. The Sanskrit root is किलकिलाय (kilakilāya).

बाबा.etym: Imitative of baby talk. Compare Persian بابا (bâbâ), Arabic بَابَا (bābā).

निहायत.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian نهایت (nihāyat), from Arabic نِهَايَة (nihāya).

आसमान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian آسمان (āsmān), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háćmā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱmō. Cognate with Sanskrit अश्मन् (aśman) and possibly English hammer. Compare Bengali আশমান (aśman), Gujarati આસમાન (āsamān), Marathi अस्मान (asmān), Nepali अस्मान (asm…

हकीकत.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian حقیقت (haqīqat), from Arabic حَقِيقَة (ḥaqīqa). Related to हक़ (haq, “right, entitlement”).

नज़र.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian نَظَر (nazar), from Arabic نَظَر (naẓar).

धोखा.etym: From a derivative of Sanskrit ध्रोक्ष्यति (dhrokṣyati, “will deceive”), from the root द्रुह् (druh), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ-. Cognate with Bengali ধোঁকা (dhō̃ka), Gujarati ધોકા (dhokā) / ધોંકા (dhõkā), Marathi धोका (dhokā), Punjabi ਧੋਖਾ (dhokhā).

निगाह.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian نگاه (nigāh). Compare Punjabi ਨਿਗਾਹ (nigāh).

फौज.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian فَوْج (fawj), borrowed from Arabic فَوْج (fawj), from فَيْج (fayj), borrowed from Middle Persian pdk'. First attested in c. 1503 as Middle Hindi فوج (fvj /⁠fauj⁠/).

नीचा.etym: Derived from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀡𑀺𑀘𑁆𑀘 (ṇicca) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-), from Sanskrit नीच (nīcá), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *niHćás (“facing down”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *niHčás, from Proto-Indo-European *ni-h₃kʷ-ós, from *ní (“down”) + *-h₃kʷ- (“facing, looking”).

उतरना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀉𑀢𑁆𑀢𑀭𑀇 (uttaraï), from Sanskrit उत्त॑रति (úttarati), from उद्- (ud-) + तर॑ति (tárati).

निकलना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀡𑀺𑀓𑁆𑀓𑀮𑁂𑀤𑀺 (ṇikkaledi), from Sanskrit *निष्कलति (*niṣkalati), passive of निष्कालयति (niṣkālayati).

शाम.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian شام (šām), from Proto-Iranian *xšáfnyah. Cognate with Sanskrit क्षप् (kṣap, “night”); despite phonetic and semantic similarity, not related to Sanskrit श्यामा (śyāmā, “night, shadow”), which derives from a different root.

जलसा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جلسه (jalsa), from Arabic جَلْسَة (jalsa). Cognate with Bengali জলসা (jolośa), Punjabi ਜਲਸਾ (jalsā).

हमेशा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian همیشه (hamēša, hamīša). Compare Bengali হামেশা (hameśa), Gujarati હંમેશાં (hammeśā̃), Punjabi ਹਮੇਸ਼ਾ (hameśā).

मौजूद.etym: Borrowed from Arabic مَوْجُود (mawjūd), possibly via Classical Persian موجود (mawjūd). Compare Punjabi ਮੌਜੂਦ (maujūd).

आवाज.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian آوَاز (āwāz). Doublet of वाक् (vāk).

उतना.etym: Formed by analogy to इतना (itnā), see वह (vah) and उस (us) for more.

मक़सद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مَقْصَد (maqsad), from Arabic مَقْصَد (maqṣad). Compare Bengali মকসদ (mokśod).

मैदान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مَیْدَان (maydān), borrowed from Arabic مَيْدَان (maydān).

अलावा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian عَلَاوَه (alāwa), from Arabic عَلَاوة (ʕalāwa), عِلَاوة (ʕilāwa).

पाना.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi पाना (pānā), पाइ (pāi), पावे (pāve), from Prakrit पावइ (pāvaï), from Sanskrit प्रापयति (prāpayati). Related to आना (ānā). Cognate with Assamese পা (pa), Bengali পাওয়া (paōẇa), Maithili पाएब (pāēb), Marathi पावणे (pāvṇe), Nepali पाउनु (pāunu), Odia ପାଇ…

आँसू.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀅𑀁𑀲𑀼 (aṃsu), from Sanskrit अश्रु॑ (áśru), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háćru, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱru, from *h₂eḱ-. Doublet of अश्रु (aśru), a tatsama.

बहना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit वहइ (vahaï), from Sanskrit वहति (váhati), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *wáȷ́ʰati, from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰeti. Cognate with Marathi वाहणे (vāhṇe), Bengali বহা (boha)/বওয়া (bôoẇa), Assamese বোৱা (büa). Distant cognate with English weigh.

मजमा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مجمع (majma'), from Arabic مَجْمَع (majmaʕ).

असर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian اثر (asar), from Arabic أَثَر (ʔaṯar).

भारी.etym: Directly borrowed from Sanskrit भारी (bhārī) or inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀪𑀸𑀭𑀺𑀕 (*bhāriga), from Sanskrit भारिक (bhārika, “heavy”). By surface analysis, भार (bhār) + -ई (-ī).

भारा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀪𑀸𑀭 (bhāra), from Sanskrit भार (bhārá).

रोना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀭𑁄𑀅𑀇 (roaï), from Sanskrit रोदि॑ति॒ (róditi), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *HráwdHti, from Proto-Indo-European *HrewdH-. Cognate with Nepali रुनु (runu).

जज़्बात.etym: Borrowed from Arabic جَذْبَات (jaḏbāt), plural of جَذْب (jaḏb) (whence जज़्बा (jazbā)).

जज़्बा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جذبه (jazba, “allure, appeal, charm”), from Arabic جَذْب (jaḏb, “attraction, seduction”), from the verb جَذَبَ (jaḏaba, “to charm, to attract”).

लौटना.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi लौटना (lauṭanā, “to return”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps a metathesis of Old Hindi उलटना (ulaṭanā, “to reverse”).

रोज़.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian روز (rōz). Cognate of Sanskrit रोचस् (rocas).

साँझ.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑀁𑀛𑀸 (saṃjhā), from Sanskrit संध्या (saṃdhyā). Cognate with Assamese সাঁজ (xãz) and Bengali সাঁঝ (shãjh). Doublet of संध्या (sandhyā).

गढ़.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀕𑀠 (gaḍha), from Sanskrit *गृध (*gṛdha, “fort”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *gʰr̥dʰás (“enclosure”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰr̥dʰ-ó-s, from *gʰerdʰ- (“to enclose”). Cognate to Gujarati ગઢ (gaḍh), Bengali গড় (goṛ).

गढ़ना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit गढइ (gaḍhaï). See there for more.

senses.gloss: bodhi tree, sacred fig, peepal, Ficus religiosa, the tree under which the Buddha gained enlightenment

पीपल.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀺𑀧𑁆𑀧𑀮 (pippala), from Sanskrit पिप्पल (pippala).

पेड़.etym: Cognate with Punjabi ਪੇੜ (peṛ). Of uncertain further origin, maybe originally referring to "projecting masses" and related to Sanskrit पिण्ड (piṇḍa, “lump, clod”).

इर्द-गिर्द.etym: Reduplication of Classical Persian گرد (gird, “round”), which is cognate with Sanskrit वर्तते (vártate, “to turn, roll”) and probably English worth.

रामायण.etym: Learned borrowing from Classical Sanskrit रामायण (rāmāyaṇa).

धोबी.etym: From धोब (dhob, “a wash”) + -ई (-ī), from Prakrit [script needed] (*dhovvaï), a passive form of Prakrit [script needed] (*dhauvati), ultimately from Sanskrit धाव् (dhāv, “to rinse, cleanse”). Cognate with Punjabi ਧੋਬੀ (dhobī), Gujarati ધોબી (dhobī), Marathi धोबी (dhobī).

राजा.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit राजा॑ (rā́jā), from राज॑न् (rā́jan), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs, from *h₃reǵ- + *-s. Doublet of राय (rāy), राणा (rāṇā), and राना (rānā).

senses.gloss: a male given name, Raja, from Sanskrit

राजा.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit राजा॑ (rā́jā), from राज॑न् (rā́jan), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs, from *h₃reǵ- + *-s. Doublet of राय (rāy), राणा (rāṇā), and राना (rānā).

senses.gloss: a male given name, Ramchandra, from Sanskrit

रामचंद्र.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit रामचन्द्र (rāmacandra). Doublet of रामचंद्रन (rāmcandran).

साल.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian سَال (sāl), from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭭𐭲 (sāl), from Old Persian 𐎰𐎼𐎭 (θ-r-d), from Proto-Iranian *carHdáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćarHáts, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-. Doublet of शरद् (śarad).

senses.gloss: Ravana; the primary antagonist of epic Ramayana, described as the Rakshasa king of Lanka
Sita (an avatar of Lakshmi) and wife of Lord Rāma

सीता.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit सीता (sītā). First attested in c. 1700 as Middle Hindi سیتا (syta /⁠sītā⁠/).

हालत.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian حالت (hālat), from Arabic حَالَة (ḥāla).

गर्भवती.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit गर्भवती (garbhavatī), from गर्भ (garbha) + -वत् (-vat), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelbʰ- (“womb”).

बढ़ना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀯𑀟𑁆𑀠𑀇 (vaḍḍhaï), from Sanskrit वर्धते (vardhate, “to grow, increase”). Cognate to Punjabi ਵੱਧਣਾ (vaddhaṇā) / وَدھݨا (vadhṇā), Marathi वाढणे (vāḍhṇe), Bengali বাড়া (baṛa), Assamese বঢ়া (borha).

भीड़.etym: Inherited from Prakrit *𑀪𑀻𑀟 (*bhīḍa) (compare 𑀪𑀺𑀟𑀇 (bhiḍaï, “to meet, fight”)), from Ashokan Prakrit *𑀪𑀺𑀝𑁆 (*bhiṭ).

senses.gloss: definite intention, resolve, will, resolution, vow

संकल्प.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit संकल्प (saṃkalpa). By surface analysis, सम्- (sam-) + कल्प (kalp).

senses.gloss: a male given name, Sankalp, from Sanskrit

संकल्प.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit संकल्प (saṃkalpa). By surface analysis, सम्- (sam-) + कल्प (kalp).

senses.gloss: double (twice the number, amount, size, etc.)
verse, line (of a holy text, especially the Rigveda)

वर्णन.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit वर्णन (varṇana), from वर्ण (varṇa) + -अन (-ana).

senses.gloss: we: first-person plural personal pronoun, plural of मैं (ma͠i)
I: first-person personal singular personal pronoun

ख़ामोश.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian خاموش (xāmōš). Compare Bengali খামোশ (khamōś), Gujarati ખામોશ (khāmoś), Punjabi ਖ਼ਾਮੋਸ਼ (xāmoś).

कोना.etym: Inherited from Sanskrit कोण (koṇa). Doublet of कोण (koṇ).

गूलर.etym: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *गुल्लर (gullara) of uncertain further origin. Cognate with Punjabi ਗੁੱਲ੍ਹਰ /گلھر (gullhar), ਗੁੱਲਰ /گلر (gullar), Gujarati ગુલર (gular), ગુલરો (gulro), ગુલેર (guler).

हटना.etym: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *हट्टइ (haṭṭaï) of uncertain origin. See there for more.

senses.gloss: to remove (especially of a physical obstacle)

हटाना.etym: Causative form of हटना (haṭnā) with the suffix -आना (-ānā).

बोल.etym: Inherited from Prakrit *बोल्ल m (bŏlla), बोल्ला f (bŏllā, “talk”). Compare बोली (bolī, “language”), बोलना (bolnā, “to say”).

ठोकना.etym: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *ठोक्कइ (ṭhŏkkaï). Cognate with Punjabi ਠੋਕਣਾ (ṭhokṇā), Gujarati ઠોકવું (ṭhokvũ), Sindhi ٺوڪَڻُ (ṭhokaṇu) / ठोकणु, Marathi ठोकणे (ṭhokṇe), Odia ଠୁକିବା (ṭhukibā), Bengali ঠোকা (ṭhōka) / ঠুকা (ṭhuka), Nepali ठोक्नु (ṭhoknu). Perhaps related to…

नेता.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit नेता (netā), nominative singular of नेतृ (netṛ, “leader”), from the root नी (nī, “to lead, to guide”).

सत्य.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit सत्य (satyá, “true; truth, reality”). Doublet of सच (sac), a tadbhava.

दाढ़ी.etym: Inherited from Prakrit दाढिआ (dāḍhiā), from Sanskrit दाढिका (dāḍhikā, “beard”). Cognate with Marathi दाढी (dāḍhī), Punjabi ਦਾੜ੍ਹੀ (dāṛhī), Bengali দাড়ি (daṛi). Equivalent to दाढ़ (dāṛh, “tusk; molar tooth”) + -ई (-ī).

खिचड़ी.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀔𑀺𑀘𑁆𑀘 (khicca) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀟- (-ḍa-) + -𑀇𑀓𑀸- (-ikā-), from Sanskrit खिच्चा (khiccā). Cognate with Bengali খিচুড়ি (khicuṛi)

पकाना.etym: Ultimately from Sanskrit पचति (pacati, “cooks”). Cognate with Nepali पकाउनु (pakāunu), Assamese পকোৱা (poküa).

हाँ.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀆𑀫𑀁 (āmaṃ), from Sanskrit आम् (ām), probably a variant of the sacred syllable ॐ (oṃ). The initial h- is emphatic, from Sanskrit हि (hi), ह (ha), or related to होना (honā). Doublet of ॐ (om).

संसार.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀲𑀁𑀲𑀸𑀭 (saṃsāra), from Sanskrit संसार (saṃsāra).

बहुत.etym: Inherited from Prakrit बहुत्त (bahutta). Doublet of बहुत्व (bahutva, “abundance”). Compare Bengali বহুত (bohut), Gujarati બહુ (bahu) and Punjabi ਬਹੁਤ (bahut) / بَہُت (bahut).

सच्चा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑀘𑁆𑀘 (sacca) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-) without cluster simplification, from Sanskrit सत्य (sátya). Compare Punjabi ਸੱਚਾ (saccā).

senses.gloss: alternative spelling of अपने आप (apne āp)

आज.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀅𑀚𑁆𑀚 (ajja), from Ashokan Prakrit 𑀅𑀚 (aja), from Sanskrit अद्य (adya), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hadyá, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁edyé, from *h₁e + *dey-. Doublet of अद्य (adya).

Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀅𑀚𑁆𑀚 (ajja), from Ashokan Prakrit 𑀅𑀚 (aja), from Sanskrit अद्य (adya), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hadyá, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁edyé, from *h₁e + *dey-. Doublet of अद्य (adya).

senses.gloss: Shri Rāma, the seventh avatar of Lord Vishnu
a male given name, Ram and Rāma, from Sanskrit

छल.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀙𑀮 (chala), from Sanskrit छल (chala).

छलना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀙𑀮𑁂𑀤𑀺 (chaledi), from Sanskrit छलयति (chalayati).

senses.gloss: a demon, a malignant deity at war with the gods in Hindu mythology; a rakshasa

राक्षस.etym: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit राक्षस (rākṣasa). Doublet of राखस (rākhas), a tadbhava.

दस.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit दस (dasa), from Ashokan Prakrit 𑀤𑀲 (dasa), 𑀤𑀰 (daśa), from Sanskrit दश (dáśa), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *dáśa, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *daća, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.

गधा.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀕𑀤𑁆𑀤𑀳 (gaddaha), from Sanskrit गर्दभ (gardabha).

तमाम.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian تمام (tamām), Arabic تَمَام (tamām). Compare Assamese তামাম (tamam), Bengali তামাম (tamam).

झंडा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀥𑀚𑁆𑀚𑀡𑁆𑀟 (*dhajjaṇḍa) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-), from Sanskrit *ध्वजदण्ड (*dhvajadaṇḍa, “flagstaff”), from ध्वज (dhvaja) + दण्ड (daṇḍa). Cognate with Bhojpuri झंडा (jhaṇḍā), Punjabi ਝੰਡਾ (jhaṇḍā) / جَھنْڈا (jhanḍā), Sindhi جھَنْڊو (jhanḍo)…

senses.gloss: a chief saint of the Jains; a Tirthankara

स्कूल.etym: Borrowed from English school. Doublet of सहना (sahnā).

छोकरा.etym: Inherited from Prakrit *छोक्कर (chŏkkara) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-). Related to छोरा (chorā) and dialectal छोहरा (chohrā). Cognate with Bengali ছোকরা (chōkra), Gujarati છોકરો (chokro), and Sindhi छोकिरो (chokiro) / ڇوڪِرو (chokiro).

senses.gloss: to interrupt; to cross (one's path); to cut off
to get across, to find a path

काटना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀓𑀝𑁆𑀝𑀇 (kaṭṭaï), from Sanskrit कर्त॑ति (kártati, “to cut”), from कृ॒न्तति॑ (kṛntáti), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kr̥ntáti. Compare Punjabi ਕੱਟਣਾ (kaṭṭaṇā).

senses.gloss: to stick, to paste, to glue

महीना.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian مَهِینَا (mahīnā, “a month; monthly pay”), from مَاه (māh, “moon”).

शामिल.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian شامل (šāmil), from Arabic شَامِل (šāmil). Compare Punjabi ਸ਼ਾਮਿਲ (śāmil), ਸ਼ਾਮਲ (śāmal) / شامل (śāml), Gujarati સામેલ (sāmel), Marathi सामील (sāmīl).

जा.etym: Inherited from Prakrit जाउ f (jāu), from Sanskrit यातृ (yātṛ) (genitive यातुः (yātuḥ)), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *HyaHtā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁yénh₂tēr ~ h₁yn̥h₂trés. Cognate with Bengali জা (ja), Konkani जाव (jāv), and Marathi जाऊ (jāū). Through Indo-European, cognate w…

छड़ी.etym: From छड़ (chaṛ) + -ई (-ī). Cognate with Punjabi ਛੜੀ (chaṛī), Gujarati છડી (chaḍī), Marathi सडी (saḍī), Bengali ছড়ি (choṛi), Nepali छडी (chaḍī).

पैदा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian پیدا (paidā). First attested as Old Hindi पैदा (paidā). Cognate with Bengali পয়দা (poẏoda).

जोश.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جوش (jōš). Compare Bengali জোস (jōs).

काना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀓𑀸𑀡 (kāṇa), from Sanskrit काण (kāṇa).

पाई.etym: Inherited from Sanskrit पादिका (pādikā, “foot, shoe, quarter”), from पाद (pāda, “foot, quarter”) + -इक (-ika, “-ic: forming adjectives”).

senses.gloss: widow (a woman whose husband has died)

विधवा.etym: Borrowed from Sanskrit विधवा (vidhávā). Doublet of बेवा (bevā).

अँगड़ाई.etym: Deverbal form of अँगड़ाना (aṅgṛānā) with the suffix -आई (-āī), ultimately derived from Sanskrit अङ्ग (aṅga, “limb”).

इस्तेमाल.etym: Borrowed from Arabic اِسْتِعْمَال (istiʕmāl). Compare Bengali এস্তেমাল (estemal), Bhojpuri इस्तिमाल (istimāl).

खलीफा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian خلیفه (xalīfa), from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa).

senses.gloss: ration (fixed amount of food or other substance granted)

गाढ़ा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀕𑀸𑀠 (gāḍha), from Sanskrit गाढ (gāḍha), from the root गाह् (gāh). Cognate with Nepali गाढा (gāḍhā), Sindhi ڳاڙهو (g̠āṛo) / ॻाढ़ो, Gujarati ગાઢું (gāḍhũ), Marathi गाढ (gāḍh), Kholosi gahro.

चादर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian چادر (čādar, čādur), itself ultimately borrowed from Sanskrit छत्त्र (chattra, “cover, umbrella”). Doublet of छाता (chātā). Compare Assamese চাদৰ (sador), Bengali চাদর (cador), Gujarati ચાદર (cādar), Marathi चादर (cādar), Punjabi ਚਾਦਰ (cādar).

senses.gloss: happy (used in greetings, e.g. happy anniversary, happy birthday)

बधाई.etym: From बधाना (badhānā) + -आई (-āī). Cognate with Gujarati વધાઈ (vadhāī).

भाभी.etym: Inherited from Prakrit *𑀪𑀸𑀩𑁆𑀪 (*bhābbha), from baby talk. Cognate with Bengali ভাবী (bhabi).

गिरना.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi गिरना (giranā), from Prakrit *𑀕𑀺𑀭𑀇 (*giraï), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“drip”). Related to गलना (galnā, “to melt, ooze”) and डिगना (ḍignā, “to falter”).

बिखरना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀯𑀺𑀓𑁆𑀔𑀭𑀤𑀺 (vikkharadi), from Sanskrit *विष्करति (*viṣkarati), related to विष्किर (viṣkira, “'scatterer', a gallinaceous bird”) and from the root कॄ (kṝ, “to scatter”).

कंधा.etym: Inherited without cluster simplification from Prakrit कंध (kaṃdha), खंध (khaṃdha), from Sanskrit स्कन्ध (skandha, “shoulder”). Compare archaic काँध (kāndh), काँधा (kāndhā). Cognate to Assamese কান্ধ (kandh), Marathi खांदा (khāndā), and Nepali काँध (kā̃dh).

पकड़ना.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi पकडि (pakaḍi), पाकडि (pākaḍi), from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *पक्कडइ (pakkaḍaï), perhaps further from Prakrit पग्ग- (pagga-, “seizes”) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀟- (-ḍa-). Cognate to Gujarati પકડવું (pakaḍvũ), Marathi पकडणे (pakaḍṇe).

पूछना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit पुच्छइ (pucchaï), पुच्छदि (pucchadi), from Sanskrit पृच्छति (pṛccháti). Cognate with Gujarati પૂછવું (pūchvũ), Marathi पुसणे (pusṇe), Kalasha phúčik, Romani pućhel. More distantly cognate with Persian پرسیدن (porsidan) and German forschen. Related to प्र…

जल्द.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جلد (jald). Compare Bengali জলদ (jolod).

जवाब.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian جواب (jawāb), from Arabic جَوَاب (jawāb). Compare Punjabi ਜਵਾਬ (javāb) / جَواب, Gujarati જવાબ (javāb), Marathi जाब (jāb), Bengali জবাব (jobab).

senses.gloss: to worry or grapple with; to rend and tear; to pull and gnaw (as an animal does its prey, or a bone, etc.)

सरहद.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian سرحد (sarhadd, “border”). By surface analysis, सर (sar) + हद (had). Compare Punjabi ਸਰਹੱਦ (sarhadda).

यकीन.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian یَقِین (yaqīn), from Arabic يَقِين (yaqīn).

senses.gloss: term of address for any male older than oneself

भैया.etym: In origin, a diminutive of भाई (bhāī, “brother”), from Sanskrit भ्रातृ (bhrātṛ), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr (“brother”).

हथेली.etym: Inherited from Sanskrit हस्ततल (hastatala) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀇𑀓𑀸- (-ikā-), from हस्त (hasta) + तल (tala). Compare हाथ (hāth).

लेन-देन.etym: Dvandva compound of लेन (len, “taking”) + देन (den, “giving”). Compare Gujarati લેણદેણ (leṇdeṇ). See Azerbaijani alış-veriş for more.

पुराना.etym: Derived from Prakrit 𑀧𑀼𑀭𑀸𑀡 (purāṇa) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-), from Sanskrit पुराण (purāṇa). Doublet of पुराण (purāṇ) and पुरान (purān).

ज़माना.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian زمانه (zamāna), from Middle Persian [script needed] (ẕmʾnk' /⁠zamānag⁠/). Compare Punjabi ਜ਼ਮਾਨਾ (zamānā) / زَمانہ (zamānh), Gujarati જમાનો (jamāno), Marathi जमाना (jamānā), Bengali জমানা (jomana).

दास्तान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian دَاسْتَان (dāstān). First attested in c. 1649 as Middle Hindi داستاں (dastaṉ).

बयान.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian بیان (bayān), from Arabic بَيَان (bayān).

अनगिनत.etym: From अन- (an-, “un-”) + गिनना (ginnā, “to count, enumerate”), with the second element influenced by गणित (gaṇit, “mathematics”).

गुलाबी.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian گُلَابِی (gulābī). By surface analysis, गुलाब (gulāb, “rose”) + -ई (-ī).
Borrowed from Classical Persian گُلَابِی (gulābī). By surface analysis, गुलाब (gulāb, “rose”) + -ई (-ī).

senses.gloss: Garha (a neighbourhood of Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, India)
Garha (a village in Raniganj tehsil, Araria district, Bihar, India)

हलका.etym: Cognate with Gujarati હલ્કું (halkũ), Nepali हलुको (haluko), Bengali হালকা (haloka), Odia ହାଳୁକା (hāḷukā), Maithili हलुक (haluk), Bhojpuri हलुक (haluk), Punjabi ਹਲ੍ਕਾ (halkā), Sindhi هلکو (halko), Marathi हल्का (halkā), हळ्का (haḷkā), and distantly, Latin levis, English light.

ज़र्दी.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian زَرْدِی (zardī, “yellowness”), from زَرْد (zard, “yellow”). By surface analysis, ज़र्द (zard) + -ई (-ī). Related to ज़र (zar) and हरा (harā).

जगह.etym: The shortening of the vowels may be due to influence from जगत् (jagat, “world”).

दौड़ना.etym: From Proto-New Indo-Aryan *दवडइ (davaḍaï), an extended form of दवइ (davaï, “to go away”) with Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀟- (-ḍa-), from Sanskrit द्रवति (drávati). Cognate with Punjabi ਦੌੜਣਾ (dauṛṇā) / دَوڑنا (dauṛṇā), Sindhi ڊوڙَڻُ (ḍoṛaṇu) / डोड़णु (ḍoṛaṇu), Gujarati દોડવું (doḍvũ),…

थामना.etym: Variant of archaic थाँभना (thāmbhnā), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀣𑀁𑀪𑀇 (thaṃbhaï), from Sanskrit स्तम्भते (stambhate), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *stámbʰatay, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *stámbʰatay, from the root Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ-. Cognate to Marathi थांबणे (thāmbṇe).

चेहरा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian چِهْرَه (čihra), from Middle Persian 𐭰𐭧𐭫𐭪𐭩 (čihrag). Doublet of चित्र (citra) and चीता (cītā). Compare Assamese চেহেৰা (sehera), Bengali চেহারা (cehara), Gujarati ચહેરો (cahero), Marathi चेहरा (cehrā), Punjabi ਚਿਹਰਾ (cihrā).

अवाम.etym: Borrowed from Arabic عَوَامّ (ʕawāmm), the plural of عَامَّة (ʕāmma, “majority”) (compare आम (ām) from عَامّ (ʕāmm)). Compare Punjabi ਅਵਾਮ (avām).

अमृतसर.etym: Borrowed from Punjabi ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ (ammritsar), from Sanskrit अमृतसरस् (amṛtasaras). By surface analysis, अमृत (amŕt, “nectar”) + सरस् (saras, “lake, pool”).

खबर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian خبر (xabar), from Arabic خَبَر (ḵabar). Compare Punjabi ਖਬਰ (khabar) / خَبَر (xabar), Nepali खबर (khabar), Gujarati ખબર (khabar), Marathi खबर (khabar), Bengali খবর (khobor), Kannada ಖಬರು (khabaru), Telugu కబురు (kaburu), Assamese খবৰ (khobor).

दरवाज़ा.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian دَرْوَازَه (darwāza). Compare Assamese দৰ্জা (dorza), Bengali দরজা (dorja), Gujarati દરવાજો (darvājo), Kashmiri दरवाज़ॖ (darawāzụ), Marathi दरवाजा (darvājā), Punjabi ਦਰਵਾਜ਼ਾ (darvāzā).

पीछा.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀘𑁆𑀙 (paccha), from Sanskrit पश्च (paśca). Cognate with Pali pacchā.

रूठना.etym: From Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀭𑀼𑀝𑁆𑀞 (ruṭṭha) + -ना (-nā, “verbal suffix”), the first element of which is from Sanskrit रुष्ट (ruṣṭa).

झंडी.etym: Inherited from Sanskrit *ध्वजदण्ड (*dhvajadaṇḍa). Doublet of झंडा (jhaṇḍā).

बिछाना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀯𑀺𑀘𑁆𑀙𑀸𑀤𑁂𑀤𑀺 (*vicchādedi), from Sanskrit विच्छादयति (vicchādayati, “uncovers, unclothes”). Cognate with Nepali बिछ्याउनु (bichyāunu).

कशमकश.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian کشمکش (kaš-ma-kaš). By surface analysis, कश (kaś, “pulling”) + -म- (-ma-) + कश (kaś) (कश (kaś) also in turn being borrowed from Classical Persian کَش (kaš)).

नापना.etym: Inherited from Prakrit णप्पइ (ṇappaï). Related to ज्ञान (jñān), ज्ञापन (jñāpan), and ज्ञापक (jñāpak). Cognate to Punjabi ਨਾਪਣਾ (nāpṇā), Odia ନାପିବା (nāpibā).

ख़ौफ़.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian خوف (xawf), from Arabic خَوْف (ḵawf).

काँपना.etym: Inherited from Sanskrit कम्पते (kampate). Cognates include Gujarati કંપવું (kampvũ), Marwari कांपणौ (kā̃mpṇau), Assamese কঁপা (kõpa).

गैर.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian غیر (ġayr), from Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr). Compare with Marathi गैर (gair) and Punjabi ਗੈਰ (gair) / غَیر (ġair).

senses.gloss: to spend, pass, live out (said of time, life etc)

तर्ज़.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian طرز (tarz), from Arabic طَرْز (ṭarz).

senses.gloss: dear son: a designation of Krishna

लाल.etym: Inherited from Sanskrit लाल्य (lālya, “to be caressed”). Cognate with Old Awadhi लाल (lāla, “woman”).

ओढ़ना.etym: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀑𑀟𑁆𑀠𑁆 (oḍḍh-), from Proto-Dravidian *uṭ- (“to wear”). Compare modern Tamil உடு (uṭu, “dress”), Malayalam ഉടുക്കുക (uṭukkuka), Kannada ಉಡು (uḍu). Cognate with Bengali ওড়না (ōṛona, “shawl”) and Assamese উৰ (ur, “put on clothes”).

Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀑𑀟𑁆𑀠𑁆 (oḍḍh-), from Proto-Dravidian *uṭ- (“to wear”). Compare modern Tamil உடு (uṭu, “dress”), Malayalam ഉടുക്കുക (uṭukkuka), Kannada ಉಡು (uḍu). Cognate with Bengali ওড়না (ōṛona, “shawl”) and Assamese উৰ (ur, “put on clothes”).

बायाँ.etym: Inherited from Old Hindi बायाँ (bāyām̐), बाँव (bām̐va), बाँवाँ (bām̐vām̐), from Prakrit वाम (vāma) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀓- (-ka-), from Sanskrit वाम (vāma, “left”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂-mó- (“deficient”). See वाम (vāma) for more.

आदतन.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian عَادَتاً (ādatan), from Arabic عَادَةً (ʕādatan), from the root ع و د (ʕ w d). By surface analysis, आदत (ādat) + -अन (-an).

महज़.etym: Borrowed from Classical Persian محض (mahz), from Arabic مَحْض (maḥḍ).
Borrowed from Classical Persian محض (mahz), from Arabic مَحْض (maḥḍ).
